How we tell our stories impacts how well people relate to our characters.
In the next lesson, students will present their revised section in the Author’s Chair.
Unit 1 Lesson 43 Student Edition
Performance Task Handout
Highlighter markers
Annotate and revise a section of your personal narratives.

Identify areas that would benefit from more vivid figurative language. Refine a selected narrative excerpt by annotating for clarity, tone, and audience, then revising with more precise vocabulary, consistent narrative cohesion markers, and improved sentence fluency supported by evidence from your own draft.
Learn how to annotate a text in order to revise texts more effectively.
Students will annotate and revise a section of their personal narratives.

Students will identify areas that would benefit from more vivid figurative language. They will refine a selected narrative excerpt by annotating for clarity, tone, and audience, then revising with more precise vocabulary, consistent narrative cohesion markers, and improved sentence fluency supported by evidence from their own draft.
Students will learn how to annotate a text in order to revise texts more effectively.
Turn and Talk
Quick Write
Turn and Talk
What section of your narrative would most benefit from revision? What are two things you can do to strengthen this section?
Why do you want to focus on this section? How will your chosen techniques strengthen the writing?

For this task, you’ll write a personal narrative and have a discussion. For your personal narrative, you’ll write about an ordinary moment—a walk home, a conversation, a mistake, or a choice—that reveals something important about who you are or how you belong. After revising a section for clear voice and strong detail, you’ll share an excerpt in our class anthology and then participate in a presentation of your excerpt and Community Dialogue, where you’ll have an opportunity to present your story and discuss why others’ stories are important. Today, we’ll begin your personal narratives.
Annotation as Revision Strategy
Directions:

Yesterday, you and your partner identified sections of strength in your writing, as well sections that would benefit from revision. Today, we are addressing the areas that would benefit from revision. We are not just editing. We are revising! Editing fixes mistakes. Revising makes writing stronger. Think of editing as sweeping and tidying a room, while revising is moving furniture around . . . maybe even taking down some walls!
Editing addresses commas, spelling, and grammar.
Revising adds clarity, details, and emotions, and addresses structural aspects such as pacing.
“How to Annotate for Revision”
Annotation: a mark on a piece of writing to note areas for revision or strength
Annotation markings:
Circle vague words, such as
upset, happy, stuff,
and
things.
Underline verbs and check their tenses. Don’t switch from past tense to present or the other way around.
Star one place where you can improve punctuation for pacing.
Put a square next to one area that might benefit from more vivid language.
In the margin, write how to revise the area.
Put a box around words that are spelled incorrectly.
Can you think of a time you annotated your own writing?
I walk home after school. I felt upset. Angela didn’t sit with me at lunch. I thought about it the whole way home.

I walked home after school, feeling the heat from my embarrassed cheeks. Angela didn’t sit with me at lunch, and that stuck in my brain like a splinter in a piece of wood. The walk home seemed so much longer.
One thing I notice about the revised section is _______.
One question I have about annotation is: _______.
Using/improving _______ strengthened the writing because _______.
Explain to a partner how annotation helps you revise for stronger writing.

Teach: Annotation
Directions:

Choose a section to revise. Ask yourself:

and

Star one place where you can improve punctuation for pacing.

Share your ideas for revision with a partner. You can respond to one another’s ideas using sentence frames:
Partner A: I want to revise this section because _______. Partner B: One idea to strengthen this section would be to _______.
Partner A: I want to revise this section because _______. Partner B: I think that section already works well because _______. Have you thought about revising _______ instead?
I agree with your decision to _______.
I wonder what would happen if you _______.
Can you explain your decision to _______?
Reflection
Self-reflect on annotating and revising a section of your writing using the
Reflection routine.
How confident are you in your ability to identify areas that would benefit from revision and then revise them?
Part B: Revise a Section of Your Personal Narrative
Revising an Excerpt
Directions:

Now you are going to take all the suggestions and ideas you have gathered in the peer review and annotation process and revise your selected section. Make sure to address the items on the annotation checklist as you revise your writing.
Follow the checklist as you annotate:
Circle vague words, such as
upset, happy, stuff,
and
things.
Underline verbs and check their tenses.
Star one place where you can improve punctuation for pacing.
Put a square next to one area that needs more vivid language.
Put a box around words that are spelled incorrectly.
After you have completed your revision, highlight the changes you made based on your annotations.
Checklist
As you revise your writing, make sure you:
Add notes and make changes that are specific to your own writing.
Replace vague or general words with more precise language.
Check that your verb tense is consistent throughout your piece.
Use punctuation (like commas, periods, or dashes) to help control the pacing of your writing.
Add descriptive details to make the setting or emotions clearer for your reader.
Quick Write
Write a short response to one of the following prompts:
One change I made that strengthened my writing was _____.
I know my revisions improved my writing because _____.
One strategy I will use in future writing is _____.
Turn and Talk
Have students review their homework from the previous lesson. Students will
Turn and Talk
with a partner (the same partner they completed the Peer Review with, if possible) to discuss what they wrote.
Ask:
What section of your narrative would most benefit from revision? What are two things you can do to strengthen this section?
The section at the beginning would most benefit from revision. I could add more descriptions and include some figurative language.
Have students respond to their partner’s ideas by asking clarifying questions.
Ask:
Why do you want to focus on this section? How will your chosen techniques strengthen the writing?
I want to focus on this section because it seems flat right now and vague. Adding description and figurative language will help the reader see the scene from my narrator’s perspective.

Tell students that today, they will annotate and revise their chosen moments in preparation for presenting their chosen excerpt. Remind students of these components of the Showcase by displaying the Showcase Performance Task prompt:

For this task, you’ll write a personal narrative and have a discussion. For your personal narrative, you’ll write about an ordinary moment—a walk home, a conversation, a mistake, or a choice—that reveals something important about who you are or how you belong. After revising a section for clear voice and strong detail, you’ll share an excerpt in our class anthology and then participate in a presentation of your excerpt and Community Dialogue, where you’ll have an opportunity to present your story and discuss why others’ stories are important. Today, we’ll begin your personal narratives.
Say:

We are at the “Revise a section for clear voice and strong detail” portion of the showcase. Today, we’ll review what it means to annotate and revise. Then you’ll revise your chosen portion to prepare to present your excerpt. If you haven’t already, make your final decisions about which section you are going to annotate and revise.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Writers revise to increase clarity and meaning. You won’t need to revise your whole narrative; you’ll work on one section. You’ll use annotation as a revision strategy.
Students will choose an excerpt to annotate and revise in preparation for Author’s Chair.
Annotation as Revision Strategy
Say these Directions:

Yesterday, you and your partner identified sections of strength in your writing, as well as sections that would benefit from revision. Today, we are addressing the areas that would benefit from revision. We are not just editing. We are revising! Editing fixes mistakes. Revising makes writing stronger. Think of editing as sweeping and tidying a room, while revising is moving furniture around…maybe even taking down some walls!
Editing addresses, commas, spelling, and grammar.
Revising adds clarity, details, and emotions, and addresses structural aspects such as pacing.
Say:
We are going to annotate our own writing to show our thinking before we revise it.
Next, introduce the idea of annotation as a revision strategy. Display:
“How to Annotate for Revision”
Annotation: a mark on a piece of writing to note areas for revision or strength
Annotation markings:
Circle vague words, such as
upset, happy, stuff,
and
things.
Underline verbs and check their tenses. Don’t switch from past tense to present or the other way around.
Star one place where you can improve punctuation for pacing.
Put a square next to one area that might benefit from more vivid language.
In the margin, write how to revise the area.
Put a box around words that are spelled incorrectly.
Say:
When we annotate, we circle places that need improvement. You will circle vague words such as
upset, happy, stuff,
and
things.

Underline verbs and check their tenses. Star one place where you can improve punctuation for pacing, and put a square next to one area that might benefit from more vivid language. These are all areas that could benefit from revision. You can also identify misspelled words. Put a box around these words. The act of marking your narrative to identify these areas is called
annotation
Ask:
Can you think of a time you annotated your own writing?
Model with a short sample section. Project the passage and then model how to annotate it.
I walk home after school. I felt upset. Angela didn’t sit with me at lunch. I thought about it the whole way home.
Say:
First, I’m going to circle vague words. I’ll circle
upset
. I could be more precise with that description. What kind of upset? Angry? Embarrassed? Hurt? In the margin, I’m going to write:
Be specific—describe this feeling.
Next, I’m going to underline the verbs. I’ll underline
walk, felt, didn’t sit, thought.
Walk is the only one in the present tense. Write
different tense
next to
walk.
It might be okay to use the present tense here, but since
felt
and
thought
are past tense, one of them needs to change. Those three verbs should match because they are happening at the same time. I’ll change
walk

to the past tense to be consistent. Next, I’ll look at punctuation. The sentences are all very short. Should I combine any to change the pacing? I’ll put a star next to the first two sentences because I think I can combine those. I’ll write
Combine
in the margin. I also think the language is kind of boring. I’ll put a square next to the whole section to remind myself to include more descriptive language. Write
Include descriptive language
in the margin. I notice that one word doesn’t look right. I’ll put a box around the word
thought
to remember to check the spelling. I can write
spelling

in the margin to remind myself. After I annotate my section, I’m ready to revise! First, I’m going to read the whole section out loud so I can think about how to revise it. It’s helpful to hear it as my audience will. This will also help me get my writing out of my head.
Here’s how I revised this section:

I walked home after school, feeling the heat from my embarrassed cheeks. Angela didn’t sit with me at lunch, and that stuck in my brain like a splinter in a piece of wood. The walk home seemed so much longer.
Say:

Notice that my revision still conveys the same ideas and isn’t much longer than the original. Also, my spelling issue resolved itself because I removed the word I had misspelled. The goal of revision is to strengthen the writing and make it more interesting to read.
Guide students in a brief discussion about the annotation process.
One thing I notice about the revised section is _______.
One question I have about annotation is: _______.
Using/improving _______ strengthened the writing because _______.

One thing I notice about the revised section is that it has more emotion in it. One question I have about annotation is: do you always have to use stars and squares? Other symbols make more sense to me. Improving verb tenses strengthened the writing, because it made it clear when the story was taking place.
Address students’ questions and concerns as you discuss the annotation process.Tell students that they will work on annotating a section from their own narrative.
Help students use annotation marks to identify specific revision targets (clarity, tone, audience) and turn those marks into concrete, sentence-level improvements.
● Define the difference: Editing = correctness; Revising = stronger meaning + clearer reader experience.
● Introduce the annotation key students will use today (circle/underline/star/square/box), and explain what each mark “tells” the writer to revise.
● Emphasize “audience check”: What will a reader see/feel/understand in this moment?
● Add cohesion markers to show sequence or shift: “At first… / Then… / Suddenly… / After that… / Finally…”
● “I circled ___ because it’s vague; I’ll replace it with ___ to show ___.”
● “I underlined my verbs and noticed ___; I will change them to ___ tense to match.”
● “I starred this spot because I want the pace to ___, so I will ___ (combine / split / add a pause).”
● “I squared this line because it needs vivid language; I will add ___ (sensory detail / simile / metaphor).”
● Student can explain 1 change using: “I revised ___ because ___.”
● Affirm that students can keep their authentic voice while revising: revision strengthens impact; it doesn’t erase identity or style.
● Model the full cycle: Read aloud → Annotate → Write margin plan → Revise 1 sentence → Reread aloud to check tone and flow.
● Revoice vague emotion words: “upset” → “hurt / embarrassed / furious / shut down.”
● Upgrade weak verbs: “went / did / got” → “slumped / darted / snapped / lingered.”
● If students only edit spelling → Prompt: “Pick 1 circle and 1 star and revise meaning + pacing.”
● If revision adds length but not clarity → Prompt: “Add 1 precise verb and 1 sensory detail instead of extra sentences.”
● If tone becomes confusing → Prompt: “Read it aloud and ask: ‘Would a reader know how I feel without me naming it?’”
● Student uses at least 3 annotation marks accurately (circle/underline/star/square/box).
● Student revision includes 1 precision vocabulary upgrade and 1 cohesion marker.
Say:
Explain to a partner how annotation helps you revise for stronger writing.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
“Annotating your writing before you revise shows you exactly what you need to address in your writing. It gives you a sort of road map to complete your revision.”
Students will understand annotation and revision techniques.
Part A: Annotate a Section of the Personal Narrative (W.6.3, W.6.3.d, L.6.1.a, L.6.3.a) (10 minutes)
Teach: Annotation
Have students annotate a section of their personal narrative, then receive peer feedback.
Give students a checklist to complete and a list of items to look for as they annotate. Review the Performance Task Handout before students begin.
Say these Directions:
You will now annotate your chosen section. Use this checklist to complete the process:
Choose a section to revise. Ask yourself:
What section lacks clarity or description?
What section feels too slow or too fast?
What section feels vague or boring?
Annotating for Revision
Choose your section.
Annotate the section:
Circle vague words, such as
upset, happy, stuff,
and
things.
Underline verbs and make sure their tenses are all the same.
Star one place where you can improve punctuation for pacing.
Put a square next to one area that needs more vivid language.
Put a box around words that are spelled incorrectly.
Before students revise, have them share their annotation ideas with a partner (ideally, the one who peer reviewed their narrative).
Say:
Share your ideas for revision with a partner. You can respond to one another’s ideas using sentence frames:
Partner A: I want to revise this section because _______. Partner B: One idea to strengthen this section would be to _______.
Partner A: I want to revise this section because _______. Partner B: I think that section already works well because _______. Have you thought about revising _______ instead?
I agree with your decision to _______.
I wonder what would happen if you _______.
Can you explain your decision to _______?

Partner A: I want to revise this section because the language feels vague. Partner B: One idea to strengthen this section is to add a metaphor that conveys how the narrator feels. Partner A: I want to revise this section because it feels slow. Partner B: I think this section already moves quickly, because the description helps me really understand the setting. Have you thought about revising the dialogue instead? I agree with your decision to use present tense verbs in your section. I wonder what would happen if you used a simile to describe how the narrator feels. Can you explain your decision to add dialogue to the section?
Support students to annotate a chosen excerpt as a “revision road map” that targets clarity, tone, pacing, and vivid language.
● Direct students to choose one excerpt they will share for Author’s Chair (a manageable section).
● Post and review the annotation checklist before students begin.
● Require a margin plan: after marking, students write 1 short revision note per mark (e.g., “replace,” “combine,” “add sensory detail”).
● Partner checkpoint (2 minutes): partners explain why they chose the section and what their marks show.
● Turn “fix pacing” into an action: “split into 2 short sentences” / “combine with because.”
● Clarify tense decisions: “present is a choice” vs. “accidental tense shift.”
● “I chose this section because ___.”
● “My circles show ___ is vague; I will change it to ___.”
● “My star shows I want the moment to feel ___, so I will ___.”
● “One strength I want to keep is ___.”
● Normalize “lots of marks” as evidence of strong writer habits and growth.
● Push specificity in plans: “add detail” → “add smell + body feeling” / “add one simile.”
● If student can’t pick a section → Prompt: “Choose the part your peer marked most OR the part you will read in Author’s Chair.”
● If marks are random → Prompt: “Find 1 vague word, 1 tense issue, 1 pacing spot, 1 vivid-language spot—and then stop.”
● If student marks everything → Prompt: “Underline only the top 2 fixes that will change the reader experience most.”
● Student identifies a clear excerpt and completes the annotation checklist.
● Student writes at least 3 margin notes that describe what they will revise.
● Student can point to 1 marked place and explain the intended reader effect.
Teacher Tip

Students may feel discouraged when they see many marks on their draft. Frame annotation as a sign of strong writing habits. All the best writers annotate their first drafts. Tell students that the more they notice, the more they are growing as writers. If students seem overwhelmed, remind them they are revising one section, not the whole narrative. Revision is about improvement, not perfection.

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Identifying What to Annotate

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Annotation

Give students a “Must-Do” checklist. Circle one vague word. Underline all verbs. Add one star where punctuation could improve pacing. Add one square where descriptive language would improve the writing. Sit with a small group and annotate one sentence together before releasing students to work independently.
Struggling with: Verb Tense
Have students highlight all the verbs in one color. Ask: Are they all happening at the same time? Past or present?
Struggling with: Provide a quick reference card
Past tense verbs: Often end in -ed, like in walked. Irregular verbs don’t end in -ed; for example, ran, felt, and thought.
Ready for extension: Impact of Revisions

Ask students to summarize what they might do differently next time during prewriting and/or drafting now that they’ve been through the peer review process. Ask: Which revision will have the biggest impact on the reader? Why? Adjusting my pacing will have the biggest impact on the reader. By shortening my sentences, I can create a sense of being rushed or anxious. Short sentences will help the reader feel that anxiousness in their body.
Reflection (W.6.5)
Self-reflect on annotating and revising a section of your writing using the
Reflection routine.
How confident are you in your ability to identify areas that would benefit from revision and then revise them?
Part B: Revise a Section of Your Personal Narrative (W.6.5, L.6.1.a, L.6.3.a) (20 minutes)

Have students revise their annotated sections. When students finish their annotations, direct them to use a highlighter to mark the changes they made. Encourage students to read aloud as they revise to check wording and pacing.
Revising an Excerpt
Say these Directions:
Now you are going to take all the suggestions and ideas you have gathered in the peer review and annotation process and revise your selected section.
Make sure to address the items on the annotation checklist as you revise your writing.
Follow the checklist as you annotate:
Circle vague words, such as
upset, happy, stuff,
and
things.
Underline verbs and check their tenses.
Star one place where you can improve punctuation for pacing.
Put a square next to one area that needs more vivid language.
Put a box around words that are spelled incorrectly.
Sample responses will vary based on each student’s writing.
Say:
After you have completed your revision, highlight the changes you made based on your annotations.
Help students convert annotations into meaningful revisions that improve clarity, tone, and audience understanding while maintaining narrative cohesion.
● Require students to revise in passes:
— Pass 1: Replace circled vague words.
— Pass 2: Fix verb tense consistency.
— Pass 3: Adjust pacing at the starred spot (combine/split/pause).
— Pass 4: Add vivid language at the square (sensory + figurative language).
● Students highlight changes after revising.
● Remind students to read aloud once midway through to check flow and tone.
● Replace “I felt ___” with showing: body cues + action + thought.
● Add cohesion markers to keep the reader oriented (time/shift words).
● Strengthen figurative language: one clear simile/metaphor tied to the narrator’s perspective.
● “Instead of ___, I revised it to ___ to show ___.”
● “I added ___ to slow down the moment and help the reader feel ___.”
● “I used ___ (Then/After/Finally) to make the sequence clearer.”
● Encourage purposeful code-switching in dialogue if it matches the narrator/character voice and remains readable for the audience.
● If revision is still vague → Prompt: “Add 1 concrete image (sound/smell/touch) + one precise verb.”
● If pacing is flat → Prompt: “Add 2 short sentences at the tense moment OR add 1 longer sensory sentence to slow it down.”
● If figurative language is forced → Prompt: “Choose a comparison from your real life (such as a splinter, a heavy backpack, a buzzing phone).”
● Student revision improves at least 1 vague word, 1 verb/tense issue, and 1 pacing decision.
● Student adds at least 1 vivid detail (sensory or figurative).
● Highlighting clearly shows where changes were made.

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Turning Annotations into Revisions

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Making revisions from annotations

Ask students to choose one annotation and revise just that sentence. Provide a sentence frame: “Instead of saying ______, I revised it to ______.” Encourage students to make one change at a time, rewriting the section after each change and marking the changes as they go. As students get more comfortable, they can make more revisions at once.
Struggling with: Example

Original section: I walk home after school. I felt upset. Angela didn’t sit with me at lunch. I thouht about it the whole way home. First change: I walked home after school. I felt upset. Angela didn’t sit with me at lunch. I thouht about it the whole way home. Second change: I walked home after school, feeling embarrassed. Angela didn’t sit with me at lunch. I thouht about it the whole way home. Third change: I walked home after school, feeling embarrassed. Angela didn’t sit with me at lunch, and that fact stuck in my brain like a splinter the whole way home.
Struggling with: Expanding detail
Struggling with: Provide a “Show, Don’t Tell” question card
Struggling with: Example
What did the character see? What did the character hear? What did the character feel in their body?
Ready for extension: Experiment with revision Ask

How does revision impact tone and mood? Try more than one revision for each annotation. For example, write two different metaphors. Use two different methods of punctuation. Use two different words to replace a vague word choice. Option 1: I walked home after school, feeling embarrassed. Option 2: I walked home after school, feeling rejected.
Checklist
As you revise your writing, make sure you:
Add notes and make changes that are specific to your own writing.
Replace vague or general words with more precise language.
Check that your verb tense is consistent throughout your piece.
Use punctuation (like commas, periods, or dashes) to help control the pacing of your writing.
Add descriptive details to make the setting or emotions clearer for your reader.

Students will annotate their chosen sections of their personal narrative.
Part B: Revise a Section of the Personal Narrative (W.6.3.B, W.6.3.D, W.6.5)

Quick Write
Have students reflect on the annotation process.
Say:
Write a short response to one of the following prompts:
One change I made that strengthened my writing was _____.
I know my revisions improved my writing because _____.
One strategy I will use in future writing is _____.
One change I made that strengthened my writing was adding a simile to describe how the narrator felt.
I know my revisions improved my writing because the story flows better now. It’s much more enjoyable to read!
One strategy I will use in future writing is circling all my verbs to make sure I am using the correct tense.
Students will reflect on the annotation process.
Instruct students to take notes in their Journal on the following prompt:
Read your excerpt out loud at least three times. You may read to a person, a pet, or practice in front of a mirror.
As you read, reflect and/or annotate your writing:
Where should you slow down or pause based on punctuation?
Does your dialogue sound natural and expressive?
Are there places where your word choice or details could be clearer for your listener?

content.text: How do ordinary moments reveal who we are and how we belong?
How does sharing stories help people understand one another?
